analytic.title: Response Time Analysis of CIL-EDF Scheduling for ROS2 Multi-threaded Executors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: ROS2 multi-threaded executors leverage the parallel computing capabilities of multi-core platforms to enhance the performance of robotic systems. To make it applicable to safetycritical domains, numerous researchers have refined its scheduling schemes to improve real-time performance. The Chain-Instance-Level Earliest Deadline First (CIL-EDF) scheduling scheme prioritizes callback instances based on the deadline of chain instances, effectively maintaining a high schedulability ratio for all chains in systems. However, for chains with a constrained deadline, previous Response Time Analysis (RTA) models tend to overestimate interference workloads, leading to a substantial deviation between the computed results and the actual Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT). In this paper, we propose a novel RTA model, which accounts for the difference in the deadline of chain instances. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves higher analytical accuracy compared to the previous model.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The Robot Operating System (ROS) has attracted growing interest in the robotics industry due to its ability to provide rapid software updates for robots. From a large number of application issues, ROS exhibits a significant deficiency in real-time performance, thereby restricting its applicability in safety-critical domains with stringent timing requirements. Therefore, the ROS community released the second generation of the system in 2017, known as ROS2 [1], which abandons the master-slave architecture in favor of the Data Distribution Service (DDS), enabling direct end-to-end communication between nodes. By eliminating the master as a single point of communication, ROS2 significantly improves real-time performance. While ROS2 offers better real-time support for robotic applications compared to ROS, it still does not fully guarantee the stringent timing constraints required for hard real-time due to limitations in the existing executor scheduling schemes.

The executor is a core component in ROS2 responsible for enabling real-time capabilities, and it comes in two types: single-threaded and multi-threaded executors. Single-threaded executors execute ready callback instances sequentially within a single thread, and multi-threaded executors distribute ready callback instances across multiple threads, allowing them to be executed in parallel.

As robotic applications become increasingly sophisticated, leveraging the parallel processing capabilities of multi-core platforms through multi-threaded executors has become crucial. Sobhani et al. [2] implemented the PiCAS scheduling scheme, originally proposed in the paper [3], on multi-threaded executors, ensuring that high-priority chains meet real-time constraints. However, this approach can cause low-priority chains to be disproportionately preempted by high-priority chains, leading to significant latency. Zhengda et al. [4] propose a Chain-Instance-Level Earliest Deadline First (CIL-EDF) scheduling scheme for multi-threaded executors; this scheme outperforms that the existing schemes, the default and PiCAS, in terms of Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) and schedulability ratio.

To ensure that ROS2 applications meet real-time constraints, Zhengda et al. [4] provide a Response Time Analysis (RTA) model for CIL-EDF. Experimental results indicate that the existing model exhibits low accuracy due to taking into account many workloads that do not cause interference. In this paper, we refine the modeling of interference workloads based on the chain instances' deadlines to improve the analytical accuracy of the RTA model.

div.head: II. ROS2 OVERVIEW
div.p: Figure 1 offers a high-level overview of ROS2. Typically, a ROS2 application is assembled from several nodes. To run these applications, nodes are assigned to executors, which handle the operating system threads responsible for executing callbacks associated with the nodes. ROS2 supports five callback types-timer, subscription, service, client, and waitable callbacks-which serve as the fundamental execution units. Timer callbacks are activated at regular intervals by system timers, while the others are triggered by external messages.

Based on ROS2's scheduling abstraction, processing chains are defined as semantic structures that emerge from the exchange of messages between callbacks across one or more nodes. Default executors do not consider the chains' temporal or resource demands when scheduling callback instances. However, many safety-critical applications-such as selfdriving systems [5]-are engineered as chains with interdependent data flows, spanning from sensing to computing to actuation, where violations of real-time constraints could lead to catastrophic consequences.

Executors use callback groups to control the parallel execution of callback instances. There are two types of callback groups: reentrant and mutually-exclusive. At runtime, the execution eligibility of instances released by callback c depends on the state of the callback group it belongs to:

div.head: IV. RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: This section introduces our proposed RTA model for chains with a constrained deadline.

Due to the executor's non-preemptive scheduling mechanism [6], preemption of a chain instance occurs only when a thread is scheduling callback instances. Once a chain instance starts executing its last callback instance, its execution process will not be interfered with by other chain instances. div.head: V. EVALUTION
div.p: We used the Foxy version of ROS2 on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS with kernel 5.4.0-26-generic running on the desktop with Intel i7-1260P@2495.994 MHz and a total memory of 16GB (four cores are used in our experiments).

The benchmark set of experiments from [4], the workload parameters for chains with constrained deadlines are presented in Table I. From Γ 0 to Γ 5 , their release periods are set to {80, 80, 120, 140, 160, 180}, and the relative deadline for each chain equals its release period. In the chain set, the first callback of the Γ 0 and Γ 1 share a common callback. For the experiment on mutually-exclusive callback groups, we set {C <3,1> ..C <3,2> } and {C <4,1> ..C <4,3> } as the same group. Figure 2 presents the comparison of observed and analyzed WCRT for chains in the experiment of [4]. Analyzed1 is the result of the RTAM analysis proposed in previous work [4], while analyzed2 is the result of our current model. We observe that analyzed1 and analyzed2 both can safely upper-bound the WCRT of chains. Analyzed2 has higher accuracy than analyzed1 in all cases. Especially in the case of CD-R(M)2, the difference between analyzed2 and analyzed1 in Γ 4 and Γ 5 is over 200, the improvement of their analysis accuracy by a factor of approximately 3.5 to 4.0 (Analysis accuracy is the difference between analyzed WCRT and observed WCRT).

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we propose an RTA model for constrained deadline chains under multi-threaded executors with the CIL-EDF scheme. The proposed model achieves significantly higher analytical accuracy compared to the existing model, especially for chains with a longer relative deadline. In the evaluation, our model provides safe WCRT estimates and achieves a maximum of 4 times improvement in analysis accuracy compared to the previous model.
